993 likes, 63 comments - cntraveler on October 6, 2026: "The 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards have arrived! This is @lalehannah here—@cntraveler’s director of special projects. Each year myself and a team of editors spend the summer pouring over the results of this annual survey, in which you, our astute readers, tell us all about your favorite hotels, resorts, islands, cities, airlines, and other experiences that made your recent travels unforgettable. We love crunching the numbers and discovering where you’ve visited and what you've loved (hint: Asia had you hooked this year). 

Start reading to discover the winners—and drop a note in the comments to share all the places around the world you can't stop talking about.".

582 likes, 9 comments - cntraveler on October 31, 2026: "Since the founding of the city, Parisians had been burying their dead in the middle of town, which led to an untenable situation: In the spring of 1780, heavy rains wrecked a burial mound at the overcrowded Les Innocents cemetery, sending a wave of decaying corpses tumbling into the building next door. The king’s solution to necrotic overpopulation? Shut down all of Paris’s graveyards and transfer all the bodies to an extensive network of underground tunnels left behind by 13th-century limestone miners—a task that took 12 years to complete.

Today, morbid-minded tourists—like our @cntraveler editorial operations manager, @tayloreisenhauer, who captured these photos—can visit @catacombesdeparis_officiel. There, you can explore about a mile of this underground labyrinth’s 200 miles of bone-lined walls, greeted by this friendly inscription: "Arrête! C'est ici l'empire de la mort" (Stop! This is the empire of death).".

624 likes, 10 comments - cntraveler on October 30, 2026: "From our Archives (and for some Halloween inspo): The Power of Travel to Transform. Following the stylish wake of Hollywood dramas about high-seas assumed identities, former style director @markreiki set sail on the Queen Victoria from @cunardline in 2008. There, @henrybourne introduced us to the characters on board:

Slide 1: The Chameleon. Guess who? An air of mystery near Geiranger, Norway.

Slide 2: The Dilettante. Ladies and gentlemen, in the Art Deco Champagne Bar, the house bubbly is Veuve Cliquot.

Slide 3: The Seductress. Mrs. Robinson, I presume? Tea on Deck 3.

Slide 4: The Bombshell. Gentlemen prefer blondes.

Slide 5: The Star. Anchors aweigh...dockside in Bergen, gateway to Norway's fjords.

Slide 6: The Comedienne. Tennis, anyone? 

Slide 7: The Starlet. Reel glamour.

Slide 8: The Vamp. Shall we dance? The Queens Room hosts high tea by day and ballroom moves by night.

Slide 9: The Diva.

Our brand was first published in 1987, and has since become a global authority on the best luxury travel experiences.".

6,126 likes, 30 comments - cntraveler on October 30, 2026: "You're in for a spooky trip that goes beyond your average ghost tour in New Orleans, Louisiana, known for its spiritual history, centuries-old cemeteries, French Quarter legends, and NOLA Halloween spirit, captured here by @nocturnalnola.

Commerce writer @jeschapel knows the best way to do it, starting with the city's roots in voodoo: a spiritual tradition shaped by West African practices, Catholicism, and the Haitian diaspora. You can dig into the history of Marie Laveau—the legendary 19th-century voodoo practitioner whose name still pops up all over the city—at @mlhouseofvoodoo in the French Quarter. Or you can take an expert-led voodoo tour, where you'll learn all about the history and how it's ingrained in the city's culture today. @voodoomuseum can also help put the traditions into context.

Be sure to also make your way to the Garden District to visit Buckner Mansion, the enormous Greek Revival house built in 1857 that American Horror Story: Coven fans will recognize as Miss Robichaux’s Academy. (It’s a private home, so you'll have to admire it from the sidewalk rather than tour inside.) You can also check into the @hotelmonteleone, a French Quarter landmark dating back to 1886 with generations of reported ghost stories, from doors said to open on their own to mysterious elevator stops. I stayed there myself and found no sign of ghosts—they do make a terribly mean martini in the lobby bar, though.

For even more Halloween spirit, attend a witch brunch at @coppervine, reserve your spot at the Endless Night Vampire Ball at the @hobnola, take an adults-only ghost tour, or visit haunted houses like @themortuary or @neworleansnightmare_.".

posts.meta_description: 8,014 likes, 36 comments - cntraveler on October 29, 2026: "Edinburgh is a city of contrasts—grand yet familiar, ancient yet constantly evolving, captured here by @rishmakhadka. In recent years, the city has welcomed a wave of new openings that sit comfortably alongside heritage favorites, offering visitors more choice than ever before. Some lean into the city’s dramatic history, with richly layered interiors and period architecture, while others embrace a sleeker, more contemporary edge. Many come with rooftop bars, whisky-stocked lounges, and front-row views of the castle or the Firth of Forth. At the link in bio, @rosieconroy1 shares the best of them, whether you're coming to town for the festivals, food, or just a weekend of wandering.".

1,190 likes, 17 comments - cntraveler on October 28, 2026: "Commerce writer @jeschapel's favorite @airbnb is a Hudson Valley retreat with a creekside hot tub and sauna:

"Getting 12 people to agree on a weekend away is an exercise in logistics. Someone wants to hike; someone else would rather browse antique shops; a few people are already asking what’s for dinner. My ideal group getaway? One that leaves room for all of it, with a house you're excited to return to in between excursions. On a recent October weekend, my friends and I—a total of six couples—found that combination at @schoonmakerretreat, tucked in the quaint Hudson Valley hamlet of High Falls.

The surrounding area seemed ripe for a fall weekend of vintage shopping, cider tasting, and lots of leaf-peeping. We lucked into a real Goldilocks window, with timing just right for trees to stand ablaze with reds, yellows, and the last bits of green. The weather was crisp, but still sunny enough to sit outside for hours, from long orchard lunches to cozy s’more nights."

Read about @jeschapel's full stay and book now at the link in bio.".

806 likes, 37 comments - cntraveler on October 28, 2026: "Hi! It’s @hannah_taking_notes, news editor at @cntraveler. On my travels this year, from luxe new ski resorts in Montana and Utah to remote eco-hotels in Costa Rica and Indigenous-owned lodges in Quebec, I couldn't help but notice two distinct types of foodies on vacation: Those who prefer to sit back and savor, and those who want dirt under their fingernails and guts on their hands.

Increasingly, hotels are catering to the latter, offering a roster of experiences that invite travelers to engage more deeply with their surroundings by foraging, fishing—and yes, even hunting—for their own food. Call it a crunchy culinary trend or an evolution of the farm-to-table movement, but, to me, it points to an instinctual desire, or craving, if you will, to reconnect with the earth and the ancient skills many of us have forgotten. To explore what this shift can tell us about the current state of food and travel, we sent writers foraging for sea urchins in California, octopus fishing in Mexico, pheasant hunting in South Dakota, and salmon fishing in Alaska. Though each journey raised its own questions around sustainability and ethics, all four offered a sense of getting closer to something: a culture, an ecosystem, a food source. Each other. Ourselves. One thing’s for sure: Luxury hospitality has gone wild, and I, for one, am here for it.".

2,760 likes, 18 comments - cntraveler on October 28, 2026: "Salem, Massachusetts turns 400 this year, and the festivities this fall (and for Halloween!) are expected to be even more extravagant. Famous for its 17th-century witch trials, the city has gained a reputation for haunted thrills, offering museums that let guests explore the infamous history as well as more upbeat Halloween-themed events all October long.

Whether you're strolling through its haunted streets, captured here by @magicinsalem, or immersing yourself in the history of the witch trials, Salem offers an unforgettable journey into the past. At the link in bio @jamie.spain and @pariwils share their guide to visiting Salem this Halloween season, including where to eat, stay, and play while you're in town.".

3,484 likes, 31 comments - cntraveler on October 27, 2026: "Anyone can visit a haunted house, but did you know you can actually stay overnight at one? Only the bravest dare to book a stay at a haunted hotel, where you can experience your very own ghostly activity in real time. 

In honor of spooky season, @jamiespain and Alex Erdekian round up some of the scariest stays in the world. From a spot in Salem, Massachusetts, to a historic castle in Denmark, these famous properties have wracked up all sorts of tragedies and legends over the decades—many of them are centuries old.

Tap the link in bio for the full list, if you dare.".
